# Rank Reversals, Not Drift: An Empirical Study of Post-Hoc Calibration Ranking Stability for One-vs-Rest Logistic Regression Under Increasing Covariate Shift on Iris and Wine Quality

## Abstract

Post-hoc recalibration is routinely applied to obtain trustworthy class probabilities, yet the stability of calibration-method rankings under distribution shift is rarely measured directly. This paper reports a controlled empirical study (capability `tabular_calibration_selective_v1`) of whether rankings of one-vs-rest logistic regression equipped with sigmoid (Platt-style) or isotonic post-hoc calibration—relative to the uncalibrated model and a majority-class baseline—remain stable as covariate-shift severity increases from 0.0 to 0.75 on two tabular datasets, **iris** and **wine_quality**. Three metric families are tracked per severity: accuracy, positive-class expected calibration error (10 equal-width bins on the designated positive class), and selective risk (AURC over ten fixed confidence thresholds). The central finding is that severity itself did not reverse within-dataset method rankings; instead, reversals occur across metrics and across datasets. g., 0.005532 at severity 0.25, [RESULT-52]) yet simultaneously the highest AURC (0.396727, [RESULT-51]), while the uncalibrated model showed exactly the opposite profile. 05 at severity 0.0, [RESULT-3]) and AURC (0.005185, [RESULT-2]), whereas sigmoid was worst on both. 534375, [RESULT-74]) at low severities. These reversals caution that no calibration method—or metric—reliably dominates under shift, and that method selection must be aligned with the deployment-relevant reliability criterion.

## Introduction

Probabilistic classifiers deployed in the wild are increasingly expected to support two downstream behaviors: calibrated probability statements and selective prediction (deferral when confidence is low). Both behaviors are fragile under distribution shift, and a large literature treats shift either by correcting estimation—e.g., improving importance estimation under covariate shift to obtain accurate prediction error [SOURCE-3]—or by aligning evaluation with deployment priorities such as calibration, label shift, and error costs [SOURCE-17]. Calibration integrity has correspondingly become an operational concern rather than a purely academic one, with explicit programs for embedding calibration practice across engineering organizations and documented accounts of accuracy and calibration failures in applied science and engineering . [SOURCE-13]

A quieter assumption persists beneath this activity: that the *ranking* of calibration methods is a stable object. If a recalibration scheme is preferred in-distribution, it is implicitly expected to remain preferred as shift severity grows. Two lines of evidence already strain this assumption. First, minimal finite counterexamples demonstrate that classification accuracy, strictly proper scoring rules, and expected calibration error are mathematically dissociable—a classifier can improve on one while degrading on another [SOURCE-2]. Second, evaluation practice itself can mis-rank methods: in a day-ahead load-forecasting study, hourly accuracy criteria failed to rank configurations by the peak-alert reliability that actually governed operational decisions, because average error hid peak risk [SOURCE-6]. If metric families dissociate in principle and evaluation criteria mis-rank in practice, then the assumption that calibration-method rankings survive increasing covariate shift deserves direct, controlled measurement rather than presumption.

This paper reports such a measurement. The study executes a frozen method contract (capability `tabular_calibration_selective_v1`) in which a set of independent one-vs-rest binary logistic regression classifiers—implemented from first principles with no external machine-learning library—is trained, combined by softmax normalization, and then equipped with one of two post-hoc calibrators fitted only on a designated positive class: a grid-searched sigmoid (Platt-style) map or an isotonic (pool-adjacent-violators) map. The calibrated and uncalibrated models, plus a majority-class baseline, are evaluated at four fixed covariate-shift severities (0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75) on two tabular datasets, **iris** and **wine_quality**, along three metric families: accuracy, positive-class expected calibration error (ECE), and selective risk measured as the area under the risk–coverage curve (AURC). The research question is deliberately narrow and falsifiable: are calibration-method rankings stable as severity increases, or do rank reversals occur in accuracy, positive-class ECE, and selective AURC?

The contributions are: (1) a frozen, fully specified, library-free protocol for comparing post-hoc calibration under controlled covariate shift on tabular data, reproduced verbatim for reproducibility; (2) a complete severity × method × metric grid of observed results on iris and wine_quality, reported with per-result provenance; (3) evidence that within each dataset the method ordering was invariant to severity, while sharp reversals occurred across metrics (ECE versus AURC on wine_quality) and across datasets (sigmoid and isotonic swap roles between iris and wine_quality); and (4) an honest negative-space account—including counter-directional severity trends and a calibration method falling below the majority-class baseline—that constrains any claim of a universally preferred calibrator.

## Related Work

**Dissociation of accuracy, proper scores, and calibration error.** The closest conceptual anchor is the collection of minimal counterexamples showing that accuracy, strictly proper scores, and expected calibration error can diverge in finite samples [SOURCE-2]. That work establishes possibility of dissociation; the present study documents its magnitude and structure under a realistic pipeline. **Evaluation alignment under shift.** A second theme concerns which quantity evaluation should optimize under shift. Aligning evaluation with clinical priorities—calibration, label shift, and error costs—changes which model one selects . [SOURCE-17] Correction-oriented work improves importance estimation under covariate shift to deliver accurate prediction error estimates [SOURCE-3], and asymmetric error structures arise naturally under class-prior shift, as in positive-unlabeled classification [SOURCE-20]. The present study deliberately brackets correction: no density ratio is estimated or applied. Instead it measures the ranking behavior of uncorrected post-hoc calibration under shift, which is the regime a practitioner faces before any correction machinery is trusted.

**Selective prediction and coverage-based evaluation.** Selective prediction analyses comparing accuracy versus coverage before and after calibration have noted that recalibration reshapes the risk–coverage relationship, not merely the reliability diagram [SOURCE-7]. Distribution-free routes to coverage guarantees under ranking, such as class-wise conformal coverage via augmented label rank calibration , provide an alternative to post-hoc probability calibration for deferral decisions.  The AURC reversals reported here extend that observation from temporal peak-risk to confidence-threshold selective risk.
** Finally, the practice of recalibrating instruments whose behavior drifts has a long metrological history: wavelength-shift self-calibration with transfer learning across analytical systems [SOURCE-11], multitemporal recalibration over stable desert sites for satellite sensors [SOURCE-15], and pattern-center-shift-induced error calibration in metrology [SOURCE-10]. These analogues share the structure of the present question—a calibration fitted under one regime and applied under a shifted one—but operate on physical rather than predictive calibration.  Unlike all of the above, this study contributes a controlled, severity-resolved, multi-metric ranking analysis for post-hoc probability calibration of tabular classifiers.

## Methodology

### Problem definition

Let $\mathcal{D} = \{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ be labeled training data with classes $\{1,\dots,K\}$, and let $+$ denote the designated positive class (the last class in sorted label order). A covariate-shift severity parameter $s \in \mathcal{S} = \{0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75\}$ indexes shifted evaluation conditions produced by the evaluation harness; metric identifiers record these as `0_0`, `0_25`, `0_5`, `0_75`. Three conditions are compared at each severity—**uncalibrated**, **sigmoid**, and **isotonic**—against a **majority_class** baseline. For a metric $\mu$ with a known preference direction, define the rank $r_s(m;\mu)$ of condition $m$ at severity $s$ on a given dataset. The research question is whether $r_s(m;\mu)$ is invariant in $s$ (ranking stability), in $\mu$ (cross-metric agreement), and across datasets.

### Executed protocol (frozen method contract, reproduced verbatim)

The following is the executed protocol of capability `tabular_calibration_selective_v1`, reproduced verbatim:

> - The base model is a set of independent one-vs-rest binary logistic regression classifiers. Each binary model is trained with full-batch gradient descent (learning rate 0.05, 1000 epochs, L2 penalty 0.001) implemented from first principles; no external machine-learning library is used. Per-class scores are combined into class probabilities by softmax normalization of the per-class logits.
> - Post-hoc calibration is fitted only for the designated positive class (the last class in sorted label order). Sigmoid (Platt-style) parameters are selected by grid search over a fixed candidate set of (a, b) values minimizing binary cross-entropy on the calibration split; an isotonic map (pool-adjacent-violators) is fitted on the positive-class probability against the indicator y = positive class. At application time only the positive-class probability is calibrated; the remaining probability mass is redistributed across the other classes proportionally to their uncalibrated probabilities.
> - Expected calibration error (ECE) is computed with 10 equal-width bins on the positive-class probability: within each bin it compares the mean positive-class probability against the empirical frequency of the positive class (y = positive class), and averages the absolute gaps weighted by bin size. It is not the standard top-class-confidence ECE.
> - The area under the risk-coverage curve (AURC) is estimated by evaluating selective risk and coverage at ten fixed confidence thresholds (0.0 to 0.9 in steps of 0.1), using the maximum class probability as the confidence score and correctness of the predicted class as the risk basis, then trapezoid-integrating those ten (coverage, risk) points. It is not an integral over the full sample ordering.

### Formal specification

**One-vs-rest training.** For each class $k$, let $\tilde{y}_i^{(k)} = +1$ if $y_i = k$ and $-1$ otherwise, and let $s_k(x) = w_k^\top x + b_k$. Each binary model minimizes the L2-regularized logistic objective

$$
J(\theta_k) \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \log\!\Big(1 + \exp\big(-\tilde{y}_i^{(k)}\, s_k(x_i)\big)\Big) \;+\; \lambda \lVert w_k \rVert_2^2, \qquad \lambda = 0.001,
$$

by full-batch gradient descent with learning rate $0.05$ for $1000$ epochs. Class probabilities are obtained by softmax normalization of the per-class logits:

$$
p_k(x) \;=\; \frac{\exp(s_k(x))}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(s_j(x))}.
$$

**Post-hoc positive-class calibration.** The sigmoid (Platt-style) calibrator maps the positive-class probability through

$$
\hat{q}_+(x) \;=\; \sigma\big(a\, p_+(x) + b\big), \qquad \sigma(z) = (1+e^{-z})^{-1},
$$

with $(a,b)$ chosen by grid search over a fixed candidate set minimizing binary cross-entropy on the calibration split.  In both cases the calibrated vector redistributes the remaining mass over the other classes:

$$
\hat{p}_+(x) = \hat{q}_+(x), \qquad \hat{p}_j(x) = \frac{1-\hat{q}_+(x)}{1-p_+(x)}\, p_j(x) \quad (j \neq +).
$$

Predictions are $\hat{y}(x) = \arg\max_k \hat{p}_k(x)$ for the calibrated conditions and $\arg\max_k p_k(x)$ for the uncalibrated condition; accuracy is the fraction correct on the shifted evaluation split.

$$

The majority-class baseline predicts a single constant class; its accuracy is the registered primary metric `baseline_accuracy`.

## Experimental Design

**Datasets (executed).** Two tabular classification datasets were executed as part of the same empirical study: **iris** (experiment_result_id = 1) and **wine_quality** (experiment_result_id = 2). No other dataset was executed, and no pooled or aggregate statistics across datasets are reported.

**Conditions and baseline.** The comparison conditions are the uncalibrated one-vs-rest logistic model, the sigmoid-calibrated model, and the isotonic-calibrated model, as specified in the frozen protocol. The baseline is `majority_class`, whose accuracy anchors all accuracy comparisons; its role in the result ledger is `baseline`, whereas all per-method results carry role `comparison`. Metric directions are fixed: higher is better for accuracy; lower is better for ECE and AURC.

**Evaluation protocol.** Each dataset is processed once per severity in $\{0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75\}$: the base model is trained from first principles, post-hoc calibrators are fitted on the calibration split (positive class only), and accuracy, positive-class ECE, and AURC are computed on the shifted evaluation split. The registered primary metric is `baseline_accuracy`; the analysis metrics are accuracy, ECE, and AURC per condition per severity. All 74 observed values, with roles, directions, and sources (`metrics.json`), are reported verbatim in the Results section.

**Ablation-style axes.** Because the method contract is frozen, the factorial structure itself supplies the ablations: (i) a *calibration ablation*—uncalibrated versus sigmoid versus isotonic—at fixed severity isolates the effect of post-hoc calibration; (ii) a *severity sweep* at fixed condition isolates shift effects, including tests of monotonicity direction per metric; (iii) a *metric-dissociation analysis* compares orderings under ECE versus AURC versus accuracy at fixed condition and severity; and (iv) a *baseline-referenced analysis* asks whether any condition's accuracy falls below the majority-class baseline. Single-run execution (one run per dataset, experiment_result_ids 1 and 2) means no seed replication is available; this is treated as a limitation rather than disguised.

## Expected Results

This section records the pre-experiment expectations that motivated the design, stated as hypotheses and explicitly not as observations; the observed outcomes in the Results section are the authoritative record.

**H1 (monotone degradation).** Increasing covariate-shift severity was expected to degrade all three metrics roughly monotonically for all conditions, on the intuition that harder evaluation conditions should reduce accuracy, worsen calibration, and raise selective risk. **H2 (calibration neutrality on accuracy).** Because calibration alters only the positive-class probability and redistributes remaining mass, argmax predictions were expected to be largely unchanged, so accuracy differences across conditions were expected to be negligible. **H3 (isotonic advantage).** The more flexible isotonic map was expected to achieve lower positive-class ECE than the two-parameter sigmoid map, with both improving on the uncalibrated model. **H4 (ranking stability).** The motivating expectation—consistent with common practice—was that condition rankings would be stable in severity, stable across metrics, and stable across datasets, so that a single calibrator could be recommended once and reused.

Justification for these expectations came from the framing that post-hoc calibration is a benign post-processing step: it fits a monotone map on a held-out split and therefore should not damage the decision rule (H2), while greater flexibility should fit the recalibration mapping more tightly (H3). The anticipated quantitative pattern was a mild, monotone worsening with severity (H1) and an ordering isotonic $\prec$ sigmoid $\prec$ uncalibrated on ECE with no ordering change on accuracy or AURC (H4). As the Results section shows, H1 fails sharply on wine_quality (all metrics improve with severity for the calibrated conditions), H2 fails on wine_quality (calibration changes accuracy enough to move one condition below the majority baseline at low severity), H3 fails on wine_quality while holding on iris, and H4 holds *within* each dataset but fails across metrics and across datasets—the central finding.

## Discussion

**Answer to the research question.** Within each executed dataset, calibration-method rankings were stable across the four covariate-shift severities for all three metric families; no severity-induced rank reversal was observed.  This aligns with the principle that accuracy, proper scores, and calibration error are dissociable [SOURCE-2], with prior observations that calibration reshapes accuracy–coverage behavior [SOURCE-7], and with evidence that evaluation criteria aligned to one characteristic can mis-rank on the reliability measure that matters [SOURCE-6].  The wine_quality accuracy gains under severity remain unexplained by the recorded outputs and motivate severity-resolved baselines in future runs.
 (ii) Evaluation splits appear small on iris: the observed accuracies equal 14/15, 12/13, and 10/11 in lowest terms across severities, implying coarse metric granularity.  (iv) Only one baseline_accuracy value per dataset was recorded, preventing severity-resolved baseline referencing.  (vi) Two datasets and one model family constrain external validity; no pooled statistics are reported, by design.  The wine-quality domain itself is low-stakes, but the protocol's structure generalizes to higher-stakes tabular prediction, where silent metric–task misalignment could cause harm; reporting rank reversals explicitly is a step toward preventing that.

## Conclusion

This paper reported a controlled empirical study (`tabular_calibration_selective_v1`) of ranking stability for post-hoc calibration of one-vs-rest logistic regression—sigmoid and isotonic positive-class recalibration versus the uncalibrated model and a majority-class baseline—under four fixed covariate-shift severities on the iris and wine_quality tabular datasets, tracking accuracy, positive-class ECE, and threshold-based selective AURC.  The practical conclusion stands on the observed record alone: under covariate shift, no calibrator in this study dominated across metrics or datasets, and method selection must follow the deployment-relevant reliability criterion.

# Rank Reversals, Not Drift: An Empirical Study of Post-Hoc Calibration Ranking Stability for One-vs-Rest Logistic Regression Under Increasing Covariate Shift on Iris and Wine Quality

## Abstract

Post-hoc recalibration is routinely applied to obtain trustworthy class probabilities, yet the stability of calibration-method rankings under distribution shift is rarely measured directly. This paper reports a controlled empirical study (capability `tabular_calibration_selective_v1`) of whether rankings of one-vs-rest logistic regression equipped with sigmoid (Platt-style) or isotonic post-hoc calibration—relative to the uncalibrated model and a majority-class baseline—remain stable as covariate-shift severity increases from 0.0 to 0.75 on two tabular datasets, **iris** and **wine_quality**. Three metric families are tracked per severity: accuracy, positive-class expected calibration error (10 equal-width bins on the designated positive class), and selective risk (AURC over ten fixed confidence thresholds). The central finding is that severity itself did not reverse within-dataset method rankings; instead, reversals occur across metrics and across datasets. g., 0.005532 at severity 0.25, [RESULT-52]) yet simultaneously the highest AURC (0.396727, [RESULT-51]), while the uncalibrated model showed exactly the opposite profile. 05 at severity 0.0, [RESULT-3]) and AURC (0.005185, [RESULT-2]), whereas sigmoid was worst on both. 534375, [RESULT-74]) at low severities. These reversals caution that no calibration method—or metric—reliably dominates under shift, and that method selection must be aligned with the deployment-relevant reliability criterion.

## Introduction

Probabilistic classifiers deployed in the wild are increasingly expected to support two downstream behaviors: calibrated probability statements and selective prediction (deferral when confidence is low). Both behaviors are fragile under distribution shift, and a large literature treats shift either by correcting estimation—e.g., improving importance estimation under covariate shift to obtain accurate prediction error [SOURCE-3]—or by aligning evaluation with deployment priorities such as calibration, label shift, and error costs [SOURCE-17]. Calibration integrity has correspondingly become an operational concern rather than a purely academic one, with explicit programs for embedding calibration practice across engineering organizations and documented accounts of accuracy and calibration failures in applied science and engineering . [SOURCE-13]

A quieter assumption persists beneath this activity: that the *ranking* of calibration methods is a stable object. If a recalibration scheme is preferred in-distribution, it is implicitly expected to remain preferred as shift severity grows. Two lines of evidence already strain this assumption. First, minimal finite counterexamples demonstrate that classification accuracy, strictly proper scoring rules, and expected calibration error are mathematically dissociable—a classifier can improve on one while degrading on another [SOURCE-2]. Second, evaluation practice itself can mis-rank methods: in a day-ahead load-forecasting study, hourly accuracy criteria failed to rank configurations by the peak-alert reliability that actually governed operational decisions, because average error hid peak risk [SOURCE-6]. If metric families dissociate in principle and evaluation criteria mis-rank in practice, then the assumption that calibration-method rankings survive increasing covariate shift deserves direct, controlled measurement rather than presumption.

This paper reports such a measurement. The study executes a frozen method contract (capability `tabular_calibration_selective_v1`) in which a set of independent one-vs-rest binary logistic regression classifiers—implemented from first principles with no external machine-learning library—is trained, combined by softmax normalization, and then equipped with one of two post-hoc calibrators fitted only on a designated positive class: a grid-searched sigmoid (Platt-style) map or an isotonic (pool-adjacent-violators) map. The calibrated and uncalibrated models, plus a majority-class baseline, are evaluated at four fixed covariate-shift severities (0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75) on two tabular datasets, **iris** and **wine_quality**, along three metric families: accuracy, positive-class expected calibration error (ECE), and selective risk measured as the area under the risk–coverage curve (AURC). The research question is deliberately narrow and falsifiable: are calibration-method rankings stable as severity increases, or do rank reversals occur in accuracy, positive-class ECE, and selective AURC?

The contributions are: (1) a frozen, fully specified, library-free protocol for comparing post-hoc calibration under controlled covariate shift on tabular data, reproduced verbatim for reproducibility; (2) a complete severity × method × metric grid of observed results on iris and wine_quality, reported with per-result provenance; (3) evidence that within each dataset the method ordering was invariant to severity, while sharp reversals occurred across metrics (ECE versus AURC on wine_quality) and across datasets (sigmoid and isotonic swap roles between iris and wine_quality); and (4) an honest negative-space account—including counter-directional severity trends and a calibration method falling below the majority-class baseline—that constrains any claim of a universally preferred calibrator.

## Related Work

**Dissociation of accuracy, proper scores, and calibration error.** The closest conceptual anchor is the collection of minimal counterexamples showing that accuracy, strictly proper scores, and expected calibration error can diverge in finite samples [SOURCE-2]. That work establishes possibility of dissociation; the present study documents its magnitude and structure under a realistic pipeline. **Evaluation alignment under shift.** A second theme concerns which quantity evaluation should optimize under shift. Aligning evaluation with clinical priorities—calibration, label shift, and error costs—changes which model one selects . [SOURCE-17] Correction-oriented work improves importance estimation under covariate shift to deliver accurate prediction error estimates [SOURCE-3], and asymmetric error structures arise naturally under class-prior shift, as in positive-unlabeled classification [SOURCE-20]. The present study deliberately brackets correction: no density ratio is estimated or applied. Instead it measures the ranking behavior of uncorrected post-hoc calibration under shift, which is the regime a practitioner faces before any correction machinery is trusted.

**Selective prediction and coverage-based evaluation.** Selective prediction analyses comparing accuracy versus coverage before and after calibration have noted that recalibration reshapes the risk–coverage relationship, not merely the reliability diagram [SOURCE-7]. Distribution-free routes to coverage guarantees under ranking, such as class-wise conformal coverage via augmented label rank calibration , provide an alternative to post-hoc probability calibration for deferral decisions.  The AURC reversals reported here extend that observation from temporal peak-risk to confidence-threshold selective risk.
** Finally, the practice of recalibrating instruments whose behavior drifts has a long metrological history: wavelength-shift self-calibration with transfer learning across analytical systems [SOURCE-11], multitemporal recalibration over stable desert sites for satellite sensors [SOURCE-15], and pattern-center-shift-induced error calibration in metrology [SOURCE-10]. These analogues share the structure of the present question—a calibration fitted under one regime and applied under a shifted one—but operate on physical rather than predictive calibration.  Unlike all of the above, this study contributes a controlled, severity-resolved, multi-metric ranking analysis for post-hoc probability calibration of tabular classifiers.

## Methodology

### Problem definition

Let $\mathcal{D} = \{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ be labeled training data with classes $\{1,\dots,K\}$, and let $+$ denote the designated positive class (the last class in sorted label order). A covariate-shift severity parameter $s \in \mathcal{S} = \{0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75\}$ indexes shifted evaluation conditions produced by the evaluation harness; metric identifiers record these as `0_0`, `0_25`, `0_5`, `0_75`. Three conditions are compared at each severity—**uncalibrated**, **sigmoid**, and **isotonic**—against a **majority_class** baseline. For a metric $\mu$ with a known preference direction, define the rank $r_s(m;\mu)$ of condition $m$ at severity $s$ on a given dataset. The research question is whether $r_s(m;\mu)$ is invariant in $s$ (ranking stability), in $\mu$ (cross-metric agreement), and across datasets.

### Executed protocol (frozen method contract, reproduced verbatim)

The following is the executed protocol of capability `tabular_calibration_selective_v1`, reproduced verbatim:

> - The base model is a set of independent one-vs-rest binary logistic regression classifiers. Each binary model is trained with full-batch gradient descent (learning rate 0.05, 1000 epochs, L2 penalty 0.001) implemented from first principles; no external machine-learning library is used. Per-class scores are combined into class probabilities by softmax normalization of the per-class logits.
> - Post-hoc calibration is fitted only for the designated positive class (the last class in sorted label order). Sigmoid (Platt-style) parameters are selected by grid search over a fixed candidate set of (a, b) values minimizing binary cross-entropy on the calibration split; an isotonic map (pool-adjacent-violators) is fitted on the positive-class probability against the indicator y = positive class. At application time only the positive-class probability is calibrated; the remaining probability mass is redistributed across the other classes proportionally to their uncalibrated probabilities.
> - Expected calibration error (ECE) is computed with 10 equal-width bins on the positive-class probability: within each bin it compares the mean positive-class probability against the empirical frequency of the positive class (y = positive class), and averages the absolute gaps weighted by bin size. It is not the standard top-class-confidence ECE.
> - The area under the risk-coverage curve (AURC) is estimated by evaluating selective risk and coverage at ten fixed confidence thresholds (0.0 to 0.9 in steps of 0.1), using the maximum class probability as the confidence score and correctness of the predicted class as the risk basis, then trapezoid-integrating those ten (coverage, risk) points. It is not an integral over the full sample ordering.

### Formal specification

**One-vs-rest training.** For each class $k$, let $\tilde{y}_i^{(k)} = +1$ if $y_i = k$ and $-1$ otherwise, and let $s_k(x) = w_k^\top x + b_k$. Each binary model minimizes the L2-regularized logistic objective

$$
J(\theta_k) \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \log\!\Big(1 + \exp\big(-\tilde{y}_i^{(k)}\, s_k(x_i)\big)\Big) \;+\; \lambda \lVert w_k \rVert_2^2, \qquad \lambda = 0.001,
$$

by full-batch gradient descent with learning rate $0.05$ for $1000$ epochs. Class probabilities are obtained by softmax normalization of the per-class logits:

$$
p_k(x) \;=\; \frac{\exp(s_k(x))}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(s_j(x))}.
$$

**Post-hoc positive-class calibration.** The sigmoid (Platt-style) calibrator maps the positive-class probability through

$$
\hat{q}_+(x) \;=\; \sigma\big(a\, p_+(x) + b\big), \qquad \sigma(z) = (1+e^{-z})^{-1},
$$

with $(a,b)$ chosen by grid search over a fixed candidate set minimizing binary cross-entropy on the calibration split.  In both cases the calibrated vector redistributes the remaining mass over the other classes:

$$
\hat{p}_+(x) = \hat{q}_+(x), \qquad \hat{p}_j(x) = \frac{1-\hat{q}_+(x)}{1-p_+(x)}\, p_j(x) \quad (j \neq +).
$$

Predictions are $\hat{y}(x) = \arg\max_k \hat{p}_k(x)$ for the calibrated conditions and $\arg\max_k p_k(x)$ for the uncalibrated condition; accuracy is the fraction correct on the shifted evaluation split.

$$

The majority-class baseline predicts a single constant class; its accuracy is the registered primary metric `baseline_accuracy`.

## Experimental Design

**Datasets (executed).** Two tabular classification datasets were executed as part of the same empirical study: **iris** (experiment_result_id = 1) and **wine_quality** (experiment_result_id = 2). No other dataset was executed, and no pooled or aggregate statistics across datasets are reported.

**Conditions and baseline.** The comparison conditions are the uncalibrated one-vs-rest logistic model, the sigmoid-calibrated model, and the isotonic-calibrated model, as specified in the frozen protocol. The baseline is `majority_class`, whose accuracy anchors all accuracy comparisons; its role in the result ledger is `baseline`, whereas all per-method results carry role `comparison`. Metric directions are fixed: higher is better for accuracy; lower is better for ECE and AURC.

**Evaluation protocol.** Each dataset is processed once per severity in $\{0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75\}$: the base model is trained from first principles, post-hoc calibrators are fitted on the calibration split (positive class only), and accuracy, positive-class ECE, and AURC are computed on the shifted evaluation split. The registered primary metric is `baseline_accuracy`; the analysis metrics are accuracy, ECE, and AURC per condition per severity. All 74 observed values, with roles, directions, and sources (`metrics.json`), are reported verbatim in the Results section.

**Ablation-style axes.** Because the method contract is frozen, the factorial structure itself supplies the ablations: (i) a *calibration ablation*—uncalibrated versus sigmoid versus isotonic—at fixed severity isolates the effect of post-hoc calibration; (ii) a *severity sweep* at fixed condition isolates shift effects, including tests of monotonicity direction per metric; (iii) a *metric-dissociation analysis* compares orderings under ECE versus AURC versus accuracy at fixed condition and severity; and (iv) a *baseline-referenced analysis* asks whether any condition's accuracy falls below the majority-class baseline. Single-run execution (one run per dataset, experiment_result_ids 1 and 2) means no seed replication is available; this is treated as a limitation rather than disguised.

## Expected Results

This section records the pre-experiment expectations that motivated the design, stated as hypotheses and explicitly not as observations; the observed outcomes in the Results section are the authoritative record.

**H1 (monotone degradation).** Increasing covariate-shift severity was expected to degrade all three metrics roughly monotonically for all conditions, on the intuition that harder evaluation conditions should reduce accuracy, worsen calibration, and raise selective risk. **H2 (calibration neutrality on accuracy).** Because calibration alters only the positive-class probability and redistributes remaining mass, argmax predictions were expected to be largely unchanged, so accuracy differences across conditions were expected to be negligible. **H3 (isotonic advantage).** The more flexible isotonic map was expected to achieve lower positive-class ECE than the two-parameter sigmoid map, with both improving on the uncalibrated model. **H4 (ranking stability).** The motivating expectation—consistent with common practice—was that condition rankings would be stable in severity, stable across metrics, and stable across datasets, so that a single calibrator could be recommended once and reused.

Justification for these expectations came from the framing that post-hoc calibration is a benign post-processing step: it fits a monotone map on a held-out split and therefore should not damage the decision rule (H2), while greater flexibility should fit the recalibration mapping more tightly (H3). The anticipated quantitative pattern was a mild, monotone worsening with severity (H1) and an ordering isotonic $\prec$ sigmoid $\prec$ uncalibrated on ECE with no ordering change on accuracy or AURC (H4). As the Results section shows, H1 fails sharply on wine_quality (all metrics improve with severity for the calibrated conditions), H2 fails on wine_quality (calibration changes accuracy enough to move one condition below the majority baseline at low severity), H3 fails on wine_quality while holding on iris, and H4 holds *within* each dataset but fails across metrics and across datasets—the central finding.

## Discussion

**Answer to the research question.** Within each executed dataset, calibration-method rankings were stable across the four covariate-shift severities for all three metric families; no severity-induced rank reversal was observed.  This aligns with the principle that accuracy, proper scores, and calibration error are dissociable [SOURCE-2], with prior observations that calibration reshapes accuracy–coverage behavior [SOURCE-7], and with evidence that evaluation criteria aligned to one characteristic can mis-rank on the reliability measure that matters [SOURCE-6].  The wine_quality accuracy gains under severity remain unexplained by the recorded outputs and motivate severity-resolved baselines in future runs.
 (ii) Evaluation splits appear small on iris: the observed accuracies equal 14/15, 12/13, and 10/11 in lowest terms across severities, implying coarse metric granularity.  (iv) Only one baseline_accuracy value per dataset was recorded, preventing severity-resolved baseline referencing.  (vi) Two datasets and one model family constrain external validity; no pooled statistics are reported, by design.  The wine-quality domain itself is low-stakes, but the protocol's structure generalizes to higher-stakes tabular prediction, where silent metric–task misalignment could cause harm; reporting rank reversals explicitly is a step toward preventing that.

## Conclusion

This paper reported a controlled empirical study (`tabular_calibration_selective_v1`) of ranking stability for post-hoc calibration of one-vs-rest logistic regression—sigmoid and isotonic positive-class recalibration versus the uncalibrated model and a majority-class baseline—under four fixed covariate-shift severities on the iris and wine_quality tabular datasets, tracking accuracy, positive-class ECE, and threshold-based selective AURC.  The practical conclusion stands on the observed record alone: under covariate shift, no calibrator in this study dominated across metrics or datasets, and method selection must follow the deployment-relevant reliability criterion.

# Rank Reversals, Not Drift: An Empirical Study of Post-Hoc Calibration Ranking Stability for One-vs-Rest Logistic Regression Under Increasing Covariate Shift on Iris and Wine Quality

## Abstract

Post-hoc recalibration is routinely applied to obtain trustworthy class probabilities, yet the stability of calibration-method rankings under distribution shift is rarely measured directly. This paper reports a controlled empirical study (capability `tabular_calibration_selective_v1`) of whether rankings of one-vs-rest logistic regression equipped with sigmoid (Platt-style) or isotonic post-hoc calibration—relative to the uncalibrated model and a majority-class baseline—remain stable as covariate-shift severity increases from 0.0 to 0.75 on two tabular datasets, **iris** and **wine_quality**. Three metric families are tracked per severity: accuracy, positive-class expected calibration error (10 equal-width bins on the designated positive class), and selective risk (AURC over ten fixed confidence thresholds). The central finding is that severity itself did not reverse within-dataset method rankings; instead, reversals occur across metrics and across datasets. g., 0.005532 at severity 0.25, [RESULT-52]) yet simultaneously the highest AURC (0.396727, [RESULT-51]), while the uncalibrated model showed exactly the opposite profile. 05 at severity 0.0, [RESULT-3]) and AURC (0.005185, [RESULT-2]), whereas sigmoid was worst on both. 534375, [RESULT-74]) at low severities. These reversals caution that no calibration method—or metric—reliably dominates under shift, and that method selection must be aligned with the deployment-relevant reliability criterion.

## Introduction

Probabilistic classifiers deployed in the wild are increasingly expected to support two downstream behaviors: calibrated probability statements and selective prediction (deferral when confidence is low). Both behaviors are fragile under distribution shift, and a large literature treats shift either by correcting estimation—e.g., improving importance estimation under covariate shift to obtain accurate prediction error [SOURCE-3]—or by aligning evaluation with deployment priorities such as calibration, label shift, and error costs [SOURCE-17]. Calibration integrity has correspondingly become an operational concern rather than a purely academic one, with explicit programs for embedding calibration practice across engineering organizations and documented accounts of accuracy and calibration failures in applied science and engineering . [SOURCE-13]

A quieter assumption persists beneath this activity: that the *ranking* of calibration methods is a stable object. If a recalibration scheme is preferred in-distribution, it is implicitly expected to remain preferred as shift severity grows. Two lines of evidence already strain this assumption. First, minimal finite counterexamples demonstrate that classification accuracy, strictly proper scoring rules, and expected calibration error are mathematically dissociable—a classifier can improve on one while degrading on another [SOURCE-2]. Second, evaluation practice itself can mis-rank methods: in a day-ahead load-forecasting study, hourly accuracy criteria failed to rank configurations by the peak-alert reliability that actually governed operational decisions, because average error hid peak risk [SOURCE-6]. If metric families dissociate in principle and evaluation criteria mis-rank in practice, then the assumption that calibration-method rankings survive increasing covariate shift deserves direct, controlled measurement rather than presumption.

This paper reports such a measurement. The study executes a frozen method contract (capability `tabular_calibration_selective_v1`) in which a set of independent one-vs-rest binary logistic regression classifiers—implemented from first principles with no external machine-learning library—is trained, combined by softmax normalization, and then equipped with one of two post-hoc calibrators fitted only on a designated positive class: a grid-searched sigmoid (Platt-style) map or an isotonic (pool-adjacent-violators) map. The calibrated and uncalibrated models, plus a majority-class baseline, are evaluated at four fixed covariate-shift severities (0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75) on two tabular datasets, **iris** and **wine_quality**, along three metric families: accuracy, positive-class expected calibration error (ECE), and selective risk measured as the area under the risk–coverage curve (AURC). The research question is deliberately narrow and falsifiable: are calibration-method rankings stable as severity increases, or do rank reversals occur in accuracy, positive-class ECE, and selective AURC?

The contributions are: (1) a frozen, fully specified, library-free protocol for comparing post-hoc calibration under controlled covariate shift on tabular data, reproduced verbatim for reproducibility; (2) a complete severity × method × metric grid of observed results on iris and wine_quality, reported with per-result provenance; (3) evidence that within each dataset the method ordering was invariant to severity, while sharp reversals occurred across metrics (ECE versus AURC on wine_quality) and across datasets (sigmoid and isotonic swap roles between iris and wine_quality); and (4) an honest negative-space account—including counter-directional severity trends and a calibration method falling below the majority-class baseline—that constrains any claim of a universally preferred calibrator.

## Related Work

**Dissociation of accuracy, proper scores, and calibration error.** The closest conceptual anchor is the collection of minimal counterexamples showing that accuracy, strictly proper scores, and expected calibration error can diverge in finite samples [SOURCE-2]. That work establishes possibility of dissociation; the present study documents its magnitude and structure under a realistic pipeline. **Evaluation alignment under shift.** A second theme concerns which quantity evaluation should optimize under shift. Aligning evaluation with clinical priorities—calibration, label shift, and error costs—changes which model one selects . [SOURCE-17] Correction-oriented work improves importance estimation under covariate shift to deliver accurate prediction error estimates [SOURCE-3], and asymmetric error structures arise naturally under class-prior shift, as in positive-unlabeled classification [SOURCE-20]. The present study deliberately brackets correction: no density ratio is estimated or applied. Instead it measures the ranking behavior of uncorrected post-hoc calibration under shift, which is the regime a practitioner faces before any correction machinery is trusted.

**Selective prediction and coverage-based evaluation.** Selective prediction analyses comparing accuracy versus coverage before and after calibration have noted that recalibration reshapes the risk–coverage relationship, not merely the reliability diagram [SOURCE-7]. Distribution-free routes to coverage guarantees under ranking, such as class-wise conformal coverage via augmented label rank calibration , provide an alternative to post-hoc probability calibration for deferral decisions.  The AURC reversals reported here extend that observation from temporal peak-risk to confidence-threshold selective risk.
** Finally, the practice of recalibrating instruments whose behavior drifts has a long metrological history: wavelength-shift self-calibration with transfer learning across analytical systems [SOURCE-11], multitemporal recalibration over stable desert sites for satellite sensors [SOURCE-15], and pattern-center-shift-induced error calibration in metrology [SOURCE-10]. These analogues share the structure of the present question—a calibration fitted under one regime and applied under a shifted one—but operate on physical rather than predictive calibration.  Unlike all of the above, this study contributes a controlled, severity-resolved, multi-metric ranking analysis for post-hoc probability calibration of tabular classifiers.

## Methodology

### Problem definition

Let $\mathcal{D} = \{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ be labeled training data with classes $\{1,\dots,K\}$, and let $+$ denote the designated positive class (the last class in sorted label order). A covariate-shift severity parameter $s \in \mathcal{S} = \{0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75\}$ indexes shifted evaluation conditions produced by the evaluation harness; metric identifiers record these as `0_0`, `0_25`, `0_5`, `0_75`. Three conditions are compared at each severity—**uncalibrated**, **sigmoid**, and **isotonic**—against a **majority_class** baseline. For a metric $\mu$ with a known preference direction, define the rank $r_s(m;\mu)$ of condition $m$ at severity $s$ on a given dataset. The research question is whether $r_s(m;\mu)$ is invariant in $s$ (ranking stability), in $\mu$ (cross-metric agreement), and across datasets.

### Executed protocol (frozen method contract, reproduced verbatim)

The following is the executed protocol of capability `tabular_calibration_selective_v1`, reproduced verbatim:

> - The base model is a set of independent one-vs-rest binary logistic regression classifiers. Each binary model is trained with full-batch gradient descent (learning rate 0.05, 1000 epochs, L2 penalty 0.001) implemented from first principles; no external machine-learning library is used. Per-class scores are combined into class probabilities by softmax normalization of the per-class logits.
> - Post-hoc calibration is fitted only for the designated positive class (the last class in sorted label order). Sigmoid (Platt-style) parameters are selected by grid search over a fixed candidate set of (a, b) values minimizing binary cross-entropy on the calibration split; an isotonic map (pool-adjacent-violators) is fitted on the positive-class probability against the indicator y = positive class. At application time only the positive-class probability is calibrated; the remaining probability mass is redistributed across the other classes proportionally to their uncalibrated probabilities.
> - Expected calibration error (ECE) is computed with 10 equal-width bins on the positive-class probability: within each bin it compares the mean positive-class probability against the empirical frequency of the positive class (y = positive class), and averages the absolute gaps weighted by bin size. It is not the standard top-class-confidence ECE.
> - The area under the risk-coverage curve (AURC) is estimated by evaluating selective risk and coverage at ten fixed confidence thresholds (0.0 to 0.9 in steps of 0.1), using the maximum class probability as the confidence score and correctness of the predicted class as the risk basis, then trapezoid-integrating those ten (coverage, risk) points. It is not an integral over the full sample ordering.

### Formal specification

**One-vs-rest training.** For each class $k$, let $\tilde{y}_i^{(k)} = +1$ if $y_i = k$ and $-1$ otherwise, and let $s_k(x) = w_k^\top x + b_k$. Each binary model minimizes the L2-regularized logistic objective

$$
J(\theta_k) \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \log\!\Big(1 + \exp\big(-\tilde{y}_i^{(k)}\, s_k(x_i)\big)\Big) \;+\; \lambda \lVert w_k \rVert_2^2, \qquad \lambda = 0.001,
$$

by full-batch gradient descent with learning rate $0.05$ for $1000$ epochs. Class probabilities are obtained by softmax normalization of the per-class logits:

$$
p_k(x) \;=\; \frac{\exp(s_k(x))}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(s_j(x))}.
$$

**Post-hoc positive-class calibration.** The sigmoid (Platt-style) calibrator maps the positive-class probability through

$$
\hat{q}_+(x) \;=\; \sigma\big(a\, p_+(x) + b\big), \qquad \sigma(z) = (1+e^{-z})^{-1},
$$

with $(a,b)$ chosen by grid search over a fixed candidate set minimizing binary cross-entropy on the calibration split.  In both cases the calibrated vector redistributes the remaining mass over the other classes:

$$
\hat{p}_+(x) = \hat{q}_+(x), \qquad \hat{p}_j(x) = \frac{1-\hat{q}_+(x)}{1-p_+(x)}\, p_j(x) \quad (j \neq +).
$$

Predictions are $\hat{y}(x) = \arg\max_k \hat{p}_k(x)$ for the calibrated conditions and $\arg\max_k p_k(x)$ for the uncalibrated condition; accuracy is the fraction correct on the shifted evaluation split.
}} \;-\; \underbrace{\tfrac{1}{|B_m|}\textstyle\sum_{i\in B_m}\mathbf{1}[y_i = +]}_{\text{empirical positive-class freq.}} \Big|.

$$

The majority-class baseline predicts a single constant class; its accuracy is the registered primary metric `baseline_accuracy`.

## Experimental Design

**Datasets (executed).** Two tabular classification datasets were executed as part of the same empirical study: **iris** (experiment_result_id = 1) and **wine_quality** (experiment_result_id = 2). No other dataset was executed, and no pooled or aggregate statistics across datasets are reported.

**Conditions and baseline.** The comparison conditions are the uncalibrated one-vs-rest logistic model, the sigmoid-calibrated model, and the isotonic-calibrated model, as specified in the frozen protocol. The baseline is `majority_class`, whose accuracy anchors all accuracy comparisons; its role in the result ledger is `baseline`, whereas all per-method results carry role `comparison`. Metric directions are fixed: higher is better for accuracy; lower is better for ECE and AURC.

**Evaluation protocol.** Each dataset is processed once per severity in $\{0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75\}$: the base model is trained from first principles, post-hoc calibrators are fitted on the calibration split (positive class only), and accuracy, positive-class ECE, and AURC are computed on the shifted evaluation split. The registered primary metric is `baseline_accuracy`; the analysis metrics are accuracy, ECE, and AURC per condition per severity. All 74 observed values, with roles, directions, and sources (`metrics.json`), are reported verbatim in the Results section.

**Ablation-style axes.** Because the method contract is frozen, the factorial structure itself supplies the ablations: (i) a *calibration ablation*—uncalibrated versus sigmoid versus isotonic—at fixed severity isolates the effect of post-hoc calibration; (ii) a *severity sweep* at fixed condition isolates shift effects, including tests of monotonicity direction per metric; (iii) a *metric-dissociation analysis* compares orderings under ECE versus AURC versus accuracy at fixed condition and severity; and (iv) a *baseline-referenced analysis* asks whether any condition's accuracy falls below the majority-class baseline. Single-run execution (one run per dataset, experiment_result_ids 1 and 2) means no seed replication is available; this is treated as a limitation rather than disguised.

## Expected Results

This section records the pre-experiment expectations that motivated the design, stated as hypotheses and explicitly not as observations; the observed outcomes in the Results section are the authoritative record.

**H1 (monotone degradation).** Increasing covariate-shift severity was expected to degrade all three metrics roughly monotonically for all conditions, on the intuition that harder evaluation conditions should reduce accuracy, worsen calibration, and raise selective risk. **H2 (calibration neutrality on accuracy).** Because calibration alters only the positive-class probability and redistributes remaining mass, argmax predictions were expected to be largely unchanged, so accuracy differences across conditions were expected to be negligible. **H3 (isotonic advantage).** The more flexible isotonic map was expected to achieve lower positive-class ECE than the two-parameter sigmoid map, with both improving on the uncalibrated model. **H4 (ranking stability).** The motivating expectation—consistent with common practice—was that condition rankings would be stable in severity, stable across metrics, and stable across datasets, so that a single calibrator could be recommended once and reused.

Justification for these expectations came from the framing that post-hoc calibration is a benign post-processing step: it fits a monotone map on a held-out split and therefore should not damage the decision rule (H2), while greater flexibility should fit the recalibration mapping more tightly (H3). The anticipated quantitative pattern was a mild, monotone worsening with severity (H1) and an ordering isotonic $\prec$ sigmoid $\prec$ uncalibrated on ECE with no ordering change on accuracy or AURC (H4). As the Results section shows, H1 fails sharply on wine_quality (all metrics improve with severity for the calibrated conditions), H2 fails on wine_quality (calibration changes accuracy enough to move one condition below the majority baseline at low severity), H3 fails on wine_quality while holding on iris, and H4 holds *within* each dataset but fails across metrics and across datasets—the central finding.

## Discussion

**Answer to the research question.** Within each executed dataset, calibration-method rankings were stable across the four covariate-shift severities for all three metric families; no severity-induced rank reversal was observed.  This aligns with the principle that accuracy, proper scores, and calibration error are dissociable [SOURCE-2], with prior observations that calibration reshapes accuracy–coverage behavior [SOURCE-7], and with evidence that evaluation criteria aligned to one characteristic can mis-rank on the reliability measure that matters [SOURCE-6].  The wine_quality accuracy gains under severity remain unexplained by the recorded outputs and motivate severity-resolved baselines in future runs.
 (ii) Evaluation splits appear small on iris: the observed accuracies equal 14/15, 12/13, and 10/11 in lowest terms across severities, implying coarse metric granularity.  (iv) Only one baseline_accuracy value per dataset was recorded, preventing severity-resolved baseline referencing.  (vi) Two datasets and one model family constrain external validity; no pooled statistics are reported, by design.  The wine-quality domain itself is low-stakes, but the protocol's structure generalizes to higher-stakes tabular prediction, where silent metric–task misalignment could cause harm; reporting rank reversals explicitly is a step toward preventing that.

## Conclusion

This paper reported a controlled empirical study (`tabular_calibration_selective_v1`) of ranking stability for post-hoc calibration of one-vs-rest logistic regression—sigmoid and isotonic positive-class recalibration versus the uncalibrated model and a majority-class baseline—under four fixed covariate-shift severities on the iris and wine_quality tabular datasets, tracking accuracy, positive-class ECE, and threshold-based selective AURC.  The practical conclusion stands on the observed record alone: under covariate shift, no calibrator in this study dominated across metrics or datasets, and method selection must follow the deployment-relevant reliability criterion.

# Rank Reversals, Not Drift: An Empirical Study of Post-Hoc Calibration Ranking Stability for One-vs-Rest Logistic Regression Under Increasing Covariate Shift on Iris and Wine Quality

## Abstract

Post-hoc recalibration is routinely applied to obtain trustworthy class probabilities, yet the stability of calibration-method rankings under distribution shift is rarely measured directly. This paper reports a controlled empirical study (capability `tabular_calibration_selective_v1`) of whether rankings of one-vs-rest logistic regression equipped with sigmoid (Platt-style) or isotonic post-hoc calibration—relative to the uncalibrated model and a majority-class baseline—remain stable as covariate-shift severity increases from 0.0 to 0.75 on two tabular datasets, **iris** and **wine_quality**. Three metric families are tracked per severity: accuracy, positive-class expected calibration error (10 equal-width bins on the designated positive class), and selective risk (AURC over ten fixed confidence thresholds). The central finding is that severity itself did not reverse within-dataset method rankings; instead, reversals occur across metrics and across datasets. g., 0.005532 at severity 0.25, [RESULT-52]) yet simultaneously the highest AURC (0.396727, [RESULT-51]), while the uncalibrated model showed exactly the opposite profile. 05 at severity 0.0, [RESULT-3]) and AURC (0.005185, [RESULT-2]), whereas sigmoid was worst on both. 534375, [RESULT-74]) at low severities. These reversals caution that no calibration method—or metric—reliably dominates under shift, and that method selection must be aligned with the deployment-relevant reliability criterion.

## Introduction

Probabilistic classifiers deployed in the wild are increasingly expected to support two downstream behaviors: calibrated probability statements and selective prediction (deferral when confidence is low). Both behaviors are fragile under distribution shift, and a large literature treats shift either by correcting estimation—e.g., improving importance estimation under covariate shift to obtain accurate prediction error [SOURCE-3]—or by aligning evaluation with deployment priorities such as calibration, label shift, and error costs [SOURCE-17]. Calibration integrity has correspondingly become an operational concern rather than a purely academic one, with explicit programs for embedding calibration practice across engineering organizations and documented accounts of accuracy and calibration failures in applied science and engineering . [SOURCE-13]

A quieter assumption persists beneath this activity: that the *ranking* of calibration methods is a stable object. If a recalibration scheme is preferred in-distribution, it is implicitly expected to remain preferred as shift severity grows. Two lines of evidence already strain this assumption. First, minimal finite counterexamples demonstrate that classification accuracy, strictly proper scoring rules, and expected calibration error are mathematically dissociable—a classifier can improve on one while degrading on another [SOURCE-2]. Second, evaluation practice itself can mis-rank methods: in a day-ahead load-forecasting study, hourly accuracy criteria failed to rank configurations by the peak-alert reliability that actually governed operational decisions, because average error hid peak risk [SOURCE-6]. If metric families dissociate in principle and evaluation criteria mis-rank in practice, then the assumption that calibration-method rankings survive increasing covariate shift deserves direct, controlled measurement rather than presumption.

This paper reports such a measurement. The study executes a frozen method contract (capability `tabular_calibration_selective_v1`) in which a set of independent one-vs-rest binary logistic regression classifiers—implemented from first principles with no external machine-learning library—is trained, combined by softmax normalization, and then equipped with one of two post-hoc calibrators fitted only on a designated positive class: a grid-searched sigmoid (Platt-style) map or an isotonic (pool-adjacent-violators) map. The calibrated and uncalibrated models, plus a majority-class baseline, are evaluated at four fixed covariate-shift severities (0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75) on two tabular datasets, **iris** and **wine_quality**, along three metric families: accuracy, positive-class expected calibration error (ECE), and selective risk measured as the area under the risk–coverage curve (AURC). The research question is deliberately narrow and falsifiable: are calibration-method rankings stable as severity increases, or do rank reversals occur in accuracy, positive-class ECE, and selective AURC?

The contributions are: (1) a frozen, fully specified, library-free protocol for comparing post-hoc calibration under controlled covariate shift on tabular data, reproduced verbatim for reproducibility; (2) a complete severity × method × metric grid of observed results on iris and wine_quality, reported with per-result provenance; (3) evidence that within each dataset the method ordering was invariant to severity, while sharp reversals occurred across metrics (ECE versus AURC on wine_quality) and across datasets (sigmoid and isotonic swap roles between iris and wine_quality); and (4) an honest negative-space account—including counter-directional severity trends and a calibration method falling below the majority-class baseline—that constrains any claim of a universally preferred calibrator.

## Related Work

**Dissociation of accuracy, proper scores, and calibration error.** The closest conceptual anchor is the collection of minimal counterexamples showing that accuracy, strictly proper scores, and expected calibration error can diverge in finite samples [SOURCE-2]. That work establishes possibility of dissociation; the present study documents its magnitude and structure under a realistic pipeline. **Evaluation alignment under shift.** A second theme concerns which quantity evaluation should optimize under shift. Aligning evaluation with clinical priorities—calibration, label shift, and error costs—changes which model one selects . [SOURCE-17] Correction-oriented work improves importance estimation under covariate shift to deliver accurate prediction error estimates [SOURCE-3], and asymmetric error structures arise naturally under class-prior shift, as in positive-unlabeled classification [SOURCE-20]. The present study deliberately brackets correction: no density ratio is estimated or applied. Instead it measures the ranking behavior of uncorrected post-hoc calibration under shift, which is the regime a practitioner faces before any correction machinery is trusted.

**Selective prediction and coverage-based evaluation.** Selective prediction analyses comparing accuracy versus coverage before and after calibration have noted that recalibration reshapes the risk–coverage relationship, not merely the reliability diagram [SOURCE-7]. Distribution-free routes to coverage guarantees under ranking, such as class-wise conformal coverage via augmented label rank calibration , provide an alternative to post-hoc probability calibration for deferral decisions.  The AURC reversals reported here extend that observation from temporal peak-risk to confidence-threshold selective risk.
** Finally, the practice of recalibrating instruments whose behavior drifts has a long metrological history: wavelength-shift self-calibration with transfer learning across analytical systems [SOURCE-11], multitemporal recalibration over stable desert sites for satellite sensors [SOURCE-15], and pattern-center-shift-induced error calibration in metrology [SOURCE-10]. These analogues share the structure of the present question—a calibration fitted under one regime and applied under a shifted one—but operate on physical rather than predictive calibration.  Unlike all of the above, this study contributes a controlled, severity-resolved, multi-metric ranking analysis for post-hoc probability calibration of tabular classifiers.

## Methodology

### Problem definition

Let $\mathcal{D} = \{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ be labeled training data with classes $\{1,\dots,K\}$, and let $+$ denote the designated positive class (the last class in sorted label order). A covariate-shift severity parameter $s \in \mathcal{S} = \{0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75\}$ indexes shifted evaluation conditions produced by the evaluation harness; metric identifiers record these as `0_0`, `0_25`, `0_5`, `0_75`. Three conditions are compared at each severity—**uncalibrated**, **sigmoid**, and **isotonic**—against a **majority_class** baseline. For a metric $\mu$ with a known preference direction, define the rank $r_s(m;\mu)$ of condition $m$ at severity $s$ on a given dataset. The research question is whether $r_s(m;\mu)$ is invariant in $s$ (ranking stability), in $\mu$ (cross-metric agreement), and across datasets.

### Executed protocol (frozen method contract, reproduced verbatim)

The following is the executed protocol of capability `tabular_calibration_selective_v1`, reproduced verbatim:

> - The base model is a set of independent one-vs-rest binary logistic regression classifiers. Each binary model is trained with full-batch gradient descent (learning rate 0.05, 1000 epochs, L2 penalty 0.001) implemented from first principles; no external machine-learning library is used. Per-class scores are combined into class probabilities by softmax normalization of the per-class logits.
> - Post-hoc calibration is fitted only for the designated positive class (the last class in sorted label order). Sigmoid (Platt-style) parameters are selected by grid search over a fixed candidate set of (a, b) values minimizing binary cross-entropy on the calibration split; an isotonic map (pool-adjacent-violators) is fitted on the positive-class probability against the indicator y = positive class. At application time only the positive-class probability is calibrated; the remaining probability mass is redistributed across the other classes proportionally to their uncalibrated probabilities.
> - Expected calibration error (ECE) is computed with 10 equal-width bins on the positive-class probability: within each bin it compares the mean positive-class probability against the empirical frequency of the positive class (y = positive class), and averages the absolute gaps weighted by bin size. It is not the standard top-class-confidence ECE.
> - The area under the risk-coverage curve (AURC) is estimated by evaluating selective risk and coverage at ten fixed confidence thresholds (0.0 to 0.9 in steps of 0.1), using the maximum class probability as the confidence score and correctness of the predicted class as the risk basis, then trapezoid-integrating those ten (coverage, risk) points. It is not an integral over the full sample ordering.

### Formal specification

**One-vs-rest training.** For each class $k$, let $\tilde{y}_i^{(k)} = +1$ if $y_i = k$ and $-1$ otherwise, and let $s_k(x) = w_k^\top x + b_k$. Each binary model minimizes the L2-regularized logistic objective

$$
J(\theta_k) \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \log\!\Big(1 + \exp\big(-\tilde{y}_i^{(k)}\, s_k(x_i)\big)\Big) \;+\; \lambda \lVert w_k \rVert_2^2, \qquad \lambda = 0.001,
$$

by full-batch gradient descent with learning rate $0.05$ for $1000$ epochs. Class probabilities are obtained by softmax normalization of the per-class logits:

$$
p_k(x) \;=\; \frac{\exp(s_k(x))}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(s_j(x))}.
$$

**Post-hoc positive-class calibration.** The sigmoid (Platt-style) calibrator maps the positive-class probability through

$$
\hat{q}_+(x) \;=\; \sigma\big(a\, p_+(x) + b\big), \qquad \sigma(z) = (1+e^{-z})^{-1},
$$

with $(a,b)$ chosen by grid search over a fixed candidate set minimizing binary cross-entropy on the calibration split.  In both cases the calibrated vector redistributes the remaining mass over the other classes:

$$
\hat{p}_+(x) = \hat{q}_+(x), \qquad \hat{p}_j(x) = \frac{1-\hat{q}_+(x)}{1-p_+(x)}\, p_j(x) \quad (j \neq +).
$$

Predictions are $\hat{y}(x) = \arg\max_k \hat{p}_k(x)$ for the calibrated conditions and $\arg\max_k p_k(x)$ for the uncalibrated condition; accuracy is the fraction correct on the shifted evaluation split.
}} \;-\; \underbrace{\tfrac{1}{|B_m|}\textstyle\sum_{i\in B_m}\mathbf{1}[y_i = +]}_{\text{empirical positive-class freq.}} \Big|.

$$

The majority-class baseline predicts a single constant class; its accuracy is the registered primary metric `baseline_accuracy`.

## Experimental Design

**Datasets (executed).** Two tabular classification datasets were executed as part of the same empirical study: **iris** (experiment_result_id = 1) and **wine_quality** (experiment_result_id = 2). No other dataset was executed, and no pooled or aggregate statistics across datasets are reported.

**Conditions and baseline.** The comparison conditions are the uncalibrated one-vs-rest logistic model, the sigmoid-calibrated model, and the isotonic-calibrated model, as specified in the frozen protocol. The baseline is `majority_class`, whose accuracy anchors all accuracy comparisons; its role in the result ledger is `baseline`, whereas all per-method results carry role `comparison`. Metric directions are fixed: higher is better for accuracy; lower is better for ECE and AURC.

**Evaluation protocol.** Each dataset is processed once per severity in $\{0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75\}$: the base model is trained from first principles, post-hoc calibrators are fitted on the calibration split (positive class only), and accuracy, positive-class ECE, and AURC are computed on the shifted evaluation split. The registered primary metric is `baseline_accuracy`; the analysis metrics are accuracy, ECE, and AURC per condition per severity. All 74 observed values, with roles, directions, and sources (`metrics.json`), are reported verbatim in the Results section.

**Ablation-style axes.** Because the method contract is frozen, the factorial structure itself supplies the ablations: (i) a *calibration ablation*—uncalibrated versus sigmoid versus isotonic—at fixed severity isolates the effect of post-hoc calibration; (ii) a *severity sweep* at fixed condition isolates shift effects, including tests of monotonicity direction per metric; (iii) a *metric-dissociation analysis* compares orderings under ECE versus AURC versus accuracy at fixed condition and severity; and (iv) a *baseline-referenced analysis* asks whether any condition's accuracy falls below the majority-class baseline. Single-run execution (one run per dataset, experiment_result_ids 1 and 2) means no seed replication is available; this is treated as a limitation rather than disguised.

## Expected Results

This section records the pre-experiment expectations that motivated the design, stated as hypotheses and explicitly not as observations; the observed outcomes in the Results section are the authoritative record.

**H1 (monotone degradation).** Increasing covariate-shift severity was expected to degrade all three metrics roughly monotonically for all conditions, on the intuition that harder evaluation conditions should reduce accuracy, worsen calibration, and raise selective risk. **H2 (calibration neutrality on accuracy).** Because calibration alters only the positive-class probability and redistributes remaining mass, argmax predictions were expected to be largely unchanged, so accuracy differences across conditions were expected to be negligible. **H3 (isotonic advantage).** The more flexible isotonic map was expected to achieve lower positive-class ECE than the two-parameter sigmoid map, with both improving on the uncalibrated model. **H4 (ranking stability).** The motivating expectation—consistent with common practice—was that condition rankings would be stable in severity, stable across metrics, and stable across datasets, so that a single calibrator could be recommended once and reused.

Justification for these expectations came from the framing that post-hoc calibration is a benign post-processing step: it fits a monotone map on a held-out split and therefore should not damage the decision rule (H2), while greater flexibility should fit the recalibration mapping more tightly (H3). The anticipated quantitative pattern was a mild, monotone worsening with severity (H1) and an ordering isotonic $\prec$ sigmoid $\prec$ uncalibrated on ECE with no ordering change on accuracy or AURC (H4). As the Results section shows, H1 fails sharply on wine_quality (all metrics improve with severity for the calibrated conditions), H2 fails on wine_quality (calibration changes accuracy enough to move one condition below the majority baseline at low severity), H3 fails on wine_quality while holding on iris, and H4 holds *within* each dataset but fails across metrics and across datasets—the central finding.

## Discussion

**Answer to the research question.** Within each executed dataset, calibration-method rankings were stable across the four covariate-shift severities for all three metric families; no severity-induced rank reversal was observed.  This aligns with the principle that accuracy, proper scores, and calibration error are dissociable [SOURCE-2], with prior observations that calibration reshapes accuracy–coverage behavior [SOURCE-7], and with evidence that evaluation criteria aligned to one characteristic can mis-rank on the reliability measure that matters [SOURCE-6].  The wine_quality accuracy gains under severity remain unexplained by the recorded outputs and motivate severity-resolved baselines in future runs.
 (ii) Evaluation splits appear small on iris: the observed accuracies equal 14/15, 12/13, and 10/11 in lowest terms across severities, implying coarse metric granularity.  (iv) Only one baseline_accuracy value per dataset was recorded, preventing severity-resolved baseline referencing.  (vi) Two datasets and one model family constrain external validity; no pooled statistics are reported, by design.  The wine-quality domain itself is low-stakes, but the protocol's structure generalizes to higher-stakes tabular prediction, where silent metric–task misalignment could cause harm; reporting rank reversals explicitly is a step toward preventing that.

## Conclusion

This paper reported a controlled empirical study (`tabular_calibration_selective_v1`) of ranking stability for post-hoc calibration of one-vs-rest logistic regression—sigmoid and isotonic positive-class recalibration versus the uncalibrated model and a majority-class baseline—under four fixed covariate-shift severities on the iris and wine_quality tabular datasets, tracking accuracy, positive-class ECE, and threshold-based selective AURC.  The practical conclusion stands on the observed record alone: under covariate shift, no calibrator in this study dominated across metrics or datasets, and method selection must follow the deployment-relevant reliability criterion.
